definition: Before drawing any deforming volume (a blob, a liquid mass, a soft body), first animate its motion as a single point — a dot moved frame by frame along a smooth arc, with spacing tuned purely by eye until the timing feels right — then draw the actual volume AROUND that already-correct dot path on a new layer/track, treating the dot as the mass's centre and letting the deforming edges lag behind and catch up to it (like a magnet pulling goo) rather than moving in perfect unison with it.
purpose: Separate the two hardest problems in soft-body/liquid animation — getting the TIMING AND ARC of the motion right, and getting the VOLUME's deformation right — into two passes, so neither has to be solved simultaneously from scratch; a wrong dot path is far faster to fix than a wrong dot path tangled up with a wrong-looking blob.
visible_effect: A soft, deforming mass appears to be pulled through space from a single leading point, with its trailing edges catching up a moment later, producing a gloopy, stretchy quality rather than a rigid shape simply translating.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: Reads as genuinely soft and liquid, because the shape visibly does not move as one rigid unit — the source (magic dot) reads as the material's effective centre of mass/energy, and everything else visibly follows it.
physical_interpretation: The dot approximates the mass's own centre of mass/momentum; treating the surrounding volume as dragged behind it (rather than rigidly attached) approximates how a real viscous material's surface lags its bulk motion.
use_cases: any soft-body or liquid effect (slime, goo, fire, smoke, water) where the overall path/timing is the harder problem to get right and can be validated cheaply before investing in detailed volume work
a beginner's first attempt at effects animation, since a single dot's spacing/arc is a small, easy problem compared to a whole deforming shape
non_use_cases: an effect whose motion is simple enough (rigid, ballistic, no lag) that a single planning pass already captures everything — the presenter's own more advanced final scene (see below) skips the explicit dot pass entirely and plans arcs directly, though the same mental model is still present

a wave/energy-transfer effect where DIFFERENT PARTS of the material move at different phases simultaneously — that needs the different technique in traveling_energy_phase_offset_not_midpoint_interpolation, not a single leading dot
interactions: traveling_energy_phase_offset_not_midpoint_interpolation (this same video) — the two techniques are named by the presenter as siblings: the magic-dot/blob technique tracks a single mass's own path, while a wave effect needs multiple phase-shifted points because energy moves through only PART of the material at a time

chain_depth_proportional_secondary_delay (v16, compiled) and drag_stretch_coupling (v14, compiled) — the same lag/catch-up idea already in the corpus for rigid chains; this entry is the same principle applied to a continuous deforming volume rather than discrete rigid links, and specifically frames it as an AUTHORING SEQUENCE (plan the path, then wrap volume around it) rather than only a measured property
squash_stretch (compiled) — the presenter's own volume-conservation rule (stretch the goo thinner as it stretches longer) is a direct restatement of this existing card, not a new finding
cadence_representation: Cadence's `ai/pose.js`/`ai/plan.js` already separate a similar concern for rigid rig motion: `line_of_action`, a volume-proxy `center_of_mass_target`, and phase authoring steps (`start`, `key_pose`, `breakdown`, `hold`, `settle`) exist independently of any one part's deformation. But Cadence has no soft-body/blob volume representation at all — a rig's parts are rigid meshes on FK/IK joints, never a deforming outline dragged behind a tracked point — so the SECOND half of this technique (drawing volume around an already-planned path, with lag) has no analogue to apply it to. The FIRST half (plan the path before the detail) is already exactly how `ai/plan.js authorMotion` is meant to be used.
control_surface: `plan_motion`/`author_motion` for the path-planning half; no Cadence surface for the volume/lag half, since there is no deformable-volume item type.
detection_and_measurement_methods: `ai/motion.js sampleMotion` on a tracked point's path (position, curvature, spacing) could validate the FIRST pass exactly as authored here; nothing measures a deforming volume's edges against that path, since Cadence holds no such volume.
generation_or_modification_methods: `author_motion`'s phase/pose steps generate the path half; the volume half is entirely outside this build's authoring surface.
failure_modes: trying to draw a correct-looking deforming volume without first locking down its underlying motion path, fighting timing and shape problems at the same time
letting the volume move perfectly rigidly with the dot instead of lagging behind it, which loses the gloopy/stretchy read entirely
over-animating fully-detached trailing material instead of the production shortcut of simply shrinking it to nothing once it has visually broken off (a related time-saving detail from the same pass)
roblox_considerations: None specific — a 2D hand-drawn technique (Procreate Dreams), not tied to Roblox.
examples: "the goal is to bring a DOT to life with animation... I'll try to keep the dot moving on a nice smooth Arc" (video @ 01:10–02:01)

"I'm going to draw a little Blobby shape around the dot... think about the dot like a magnet and it's pulling this goo around as the dot moves faster some of the goo might take a moment to catch up to the dot" (video @ 02:49–03:12)
"you can think about breaking parts of the goo off that get left behind... I've just let them slowly shrink down to nothing so I don't have to keep animating them" (video @ 03:43–03:50)
evidence_status: video: https://youtu.be/VjAbB9492VA @ 01:10–03:50 — Alex Grigg demonstrates the full dot-then-blob sequence live in Procreate Dreams, confirmed in this session's own frame reads of the dot being drawn in flipbook mode; experimental until validated
